title: Sherpa Tensing — Camp Thirteen: Future Perfect Continuous (C1)
description: The last camp on the ridge, and the longest verb form in English. Stand at a point in the future, look back, and measure: by the time you get there, this…

hero.h1: The hours you'll have put in
hero.lede: The last camp on the ridge, and the longest verb form in English. Stand at a point in the future, look back, and measure: by the time you get there, this will have been going on for a stretch you can name. The stretch is the whole point.

cards.head: How long, by a future point
cards.body: The activity will have been running for a measurable stretch when you get there.
cards.ex: "By June we will have been living here ten years."

cards.head: The activity, not the result
cards.body: What fills the time, rather than what comes out of it.
cards.ex: "At six I will have been driving for eight hours."

cards.head: The cause of a future state
cards.body: Explaining in advance why somebody will be in the state they are in.
cards.ex: "She'll be shattered. She will have been travelling all night."

cards.head: It needs a duration
cards.body: Without for, since or all day, the sentence has nothing to say.
cards.ex: "By then I will have been waiting two hours."

cards.head: Never with state verbs
cards.body: A state cannot be in progress, so camp twelve takes it.
cards.ex: "I will have known her twenty years." not "been knowing"

cards.head: Rare aloud, precise on paper
cards.body: You will meet it in contracts, plans and reports far more than in conversation.
cards.ex: "By completion the team will have been working on it for three years."

cards.head: Yes / No questions
cards.ex: "Will you have been driving all day?"

cards.head: Wh- questions
cards.body: How long + will + subject + have been + -ing?

charts.head: Four pieces, in this order, always
charts.note: This is the longest verb form in English and the least troublesome, because not one of the four pieces ever changes. Learn the order and you have learnt the tense.

head: Piece
What it does
Changes?
rows: looks back from that future point
makes it perfect and continuous at once

charts.head: Conjugation chart
charts.note: The same for everybody, which is the one mercy this tense offers.

charts.head: Three mistakes worth naming
charts.note: Almost every error with this tense is one of these three.

head: Not this
This
Why
rows: By June I will have been living here.
By June I will have been living here for ten years.
Without a duration the tense has nothing to measure, and the sentence sounds unfinished.
I will have been knowing her twenty years.
I will have known her twenty years.
State verbs refuse the continuous, so camp twelve takes it.
By six I will have been writing three reports.
By six I will have written three reports.
A number is a result, and results belong to camp twelve.

charts.note: Camp twelve and camp thirteen both look back from a future point. Camp twelve counts what is finished; camp thirteen counts how long it has taken. Almost always, a number of things means twelve and a length of time means thirteen.

head: Question
Future perfect continuous
Future perfect
rows:
A length of time.
"I will have been driving eight hours."

A number of finished things.
"I will have driven four hundred miles."
Not necessarily — and it does not matter.
Yes. Without one it makes no sense.
Always. "I will have known her twenty years."

charts.example: The pair that shows the whole difference: "By six I will have written three reports" — here is what you can put on my desk. "By six I will have been writing for eight hours" — here is why I am not writing a fourth.

sections.example: A useful habit: say the sentence and listen for a length of time. If there isn't one, you want camp twelve instead — this tense cannot stand up without a duration to lean on.

diagram.intro: The trail starts at a brown past simple peg, runs straight through NOW without pausing, and keeps going to the dashed appointment on the right. That is the whole idea: the activity is already under way and it does not stop when you get there. The grey zone above is the total it will have reached by that moment — the ten years, the eight hours, whatever the sentence is really about. Click either shape to see it in a sentence.

items: By June we will have been living here …
At six I will have been driving …
By completion they will have been working on it …

panels.head: The total — how long, by then

quiz.prompt: By June we _____ here for ten years. (live)
quiz.hint: A length of time by a future point.
quiz.explain: For ten years is a duration measured to a future moment, which is exactly this tense.

quiz.prompt: At six I _____ for eight hours. (drive)
quiz.explain: Eight hours is a length of time, so the continuous. Will have driven would want a number of miles.

quiz.prompt: She'll be shattered — she _____ all night. (travel)
quiz.explain: The exhaustion is caused by how long the travelling ran, which is the continuous's job.
A number is a result, and results take camp twelve. The continuous counts hours, not reports.

quiz.prompt: Next year I _____ her for twenty years. (know)
quiz.explain: Know is a state verb and refuses the continuous, so the future perfect simple takes the duration.

quiz.prompt: How long _____ you _____ by the time you retire? (teach)
quiz.hint: The question this tense was made for.
quiz.explain: How long + will have been + -ing asks for a duration reaching a future point.

quiz.prompt: By then the machine _____ non-stop for a month. (run)
quiz.hint: A stretch, right up to that point.
quiz.explain: For a month is a duration, so the continuous. Will have run would suggest a finished job.

quiz.prompt: It _____ long by the time we get there. (not / rain)
quiz.explain: Won't have been + -ing keeps the focus on how long the rain will have run.

quiz.prompt: By completion the team _____ on it for three years. (work)
quiz.explain: For three years is a duration measured to a future completion date: future perfect continuous.

quiz.prompt: This time next week I _____ on a beach. (lie)
quiz.explain: There is no length of time to measure, only a future moment, so camp nine is right: I will be lying there.

quiz.prompt: By the end of the season they _____ for eleven months solid. (tour)
quiz.hint: A long stretch, ending at a future point.
quiz.explain: Eleven months solid is a duration reaching a future moment, so the continuous.

quiz.prompt: By Friday we _____ every room in the building. (paint)
quiz.explain: Every room is a quantity of finished work, so camp twelve takes it.

quiz.prompt: When you land, I _____ for two hours. (wait)
quiz.hint: How long, at that future moment.
quiz.explain: For two hours is a duration measured to the moment you land: future perfect continuous.

quiz.prompt: By 2040 the glacier _____ for a century. (retreat)
quiz.hint: A stretch measured to a future date.
quiz.explain: For a century is a duration, so the continuous keeps the process rather than the outcome in view.

results: Clean run. You can hear a length of time from a number of things, and you never leave this tense without a duration.
Solid progress. Worth a look back at camp eight and camp twelve.
Good first attempt. The continuous/simple fork is the part to read again.
